title: Clinical Skills
tagline: Communication, history taking, physical examination, clinical reasoning and interpreting tests
summary: Diagnosis starts with talking to and examining the patient. This course covers communication and history taking, physical examination, clinical reasoning and differential diagnosis, the interpretation of laboratory tests and medical imaging, records and handover, and patient safety.
overview: Medicine is practised through conversations, examinations, results and notes. A diagnosis is usually made in the first ten minutes of a history; a deterioration is usually survived or missed in the first ten; and most serious harm in modern hospitals traces, on analysis, to a communication failure rather than unknown science. This course treats those skills — talking, examining, reasoning, investigating, recording and handing over — as teachable, testable and as important as any basic science.

It starts with communication: explaining, listening, breaking bad news, taking a history that is both humane and diagnostic. It then moves to the physical examination, taught system by system with the same discipline: inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate, and know what each sign's sensitivity and specificity actually are. Clinical reasoning comes next — how hypotheses form, how Bayes' theorem lies behind every test request, and how cognitive biases derail good data. Laboratory and imaging chapters explain how to choose and read investigations: full blood count and chemistry, blood gases, urinalysis, inflammatory markers, the plain radiograph, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and when imaging harms.

The final chapters cover the infrastructure of safe practice: records and handover, and patient safety — error taxonomies, human factors, incident reporting, checklists and just culture. Every chapter uses worked examples, common pitfalls and quick checks, because these skills are learned by being practised against explicit standards and feedback, not absorbed by osmosis on a ward round.
outcomes: Structure a full medical history and communicate with patients across common challenging situations — explaining, eliciting the agenda, breaking bad news and exploring concordance.
Perform and present a systematic examination of each major system, and interpret the cardinal signs, stating what each sign does and does not exclude.
Apply models of clinical reasoning — hypothesis-driven and Bayes-based — and recognise the cognitive biases (anchoring, premature closure, availability) that produce diagnostic error.
Choose, perform and interpret core laboratory tests and blood gases, and understand reference ranges, predictive values and cause-and-effect of common derangements.
Interpret basic imaging: chest and abdominal radiographs, CT appearances of common emergencies, ultrasound indications and limitations, and MRI contrast principles.
Write problem-based notes and structured handovers (SBAR-style), and use tools such as problem lists and medication reconciliation to prevent information loss.
Describe the human-factors basis of patient safety, the main contributors to harm in hospitals, and countermeasures: checklists, reporting systems, escalation culture and formulary safeguards.
Practise giving and receiving constructive feedback and presenting a concise, accurate summary of a patient to a senior colleague.

history.title: The bedside as method
history.detail: The Hippocratic writings put observation and the recorded history at the centre of medicine: the epidemic notebooks describe individual cases with their course, and the physician's own demeanour and speech at the bedside are treated as part of the treatment.

history.title: Indirect listening
history.detail: Laennec's cylinder of rolled paper becomes the monaural stethoscope, and with it the idea that external signs — sounds, murmurs, rubs — stand in lawful relation to internal disease, so that the living patient can be examined as carefully as a cadaver.

history.title: The clinical method taught
history.detail: William Osler's textbook and, more influentially, his bedside clinic at the new Johns Hopkins Hospital make the graded, presented case the unit of clinical teaching — students learn by taking the history themselves under questioning that climbs from symptom to sign to diagnosis.

history.title: The intelligence of the examination
history.detail: Osler's tradition is formalised in the differential diagnosis: Joseph Yale Johnston's 'The Method in Medicine' argues that a disciplined examination, not the laboratory, remains the generator of hypotheses, a claim still worth testing against every normal blood test.

history.title: The doctor, his patient and the illness
history.detail: Michael Balint's weekly seminar for GP principals, and the book that followed, put the relationship itself — the drug 'doctor', the patient who presents by symptom rather than disease — on the clinical curriculum, ancestor of today's Balint groups and communication teaching.

history.title: To err is human
history.detail: A report for the US Institute of Medicine reviews the evidence on preventable adverse events in hospitals and reframes error as a system property — latent conditions and active failures — shifting improvement from blaming individuals to redesigning processes.

history.title: Handover made structured
history.detail: Adapted from aviation crew resource management and popularised by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, SBAR (situation, background, assessment, recommendation) becomes the standard structure for clinical handover and escalation in hospitals worldwide.

history.title: The checklist
history.detail: The World Health Organization's Surgical Safety Checklist, piloted in eight hospitals, reduces mortality and complications in a controlled before-and-after study; the lesson generalises: a short, structured, spoken confirmation at defined moments prevents omissions that memory alone will commit.
